m27.title: Ephemeral containers and disposable environments — making evidence outlive the environment
m27.mentor: CI runners, containers and preview environments are born, work and die. Whatever you didn't get out before they die is gone, and whatever you didn't pin you won't be able to repeat. There's a real case that shows it: a scientific recomputation run by an AI assistant on an ephemeral executor, where one run's arrays were lost and the fingerprints and hashes that had been stored outside survived.
m27.kid: It's like a sandcastle: the tide washes it away. If you take a photo first and write down how you built it, tomorrow you can prove it existed and build it again exactly the same.
obj: Say what gets lost when a runner or container dies, and design the run so the evidence gets out first.
Pin the inputs (lockfile, tool version, commit, digest and the data's SHA256SUMS) and show it in the log.
Resume an interrupted run from atomic checkpoints under flock without repeating work or running twice.
Verify on a clean runner and get the same fingerprint after killing and relaunching.
m27.pre: Pipelines (previous module), basic Docker, bash and SHA-256 hashes with sha256sum.
theory: What's ephemeral: a GitHub Actions hosted runner (each job starts on a clean machine that's thrown away at the end), a Docker container (its writable layer dies with it), a devcontainer (the development environment declared in .devcontainer/devcontainer.json, rebuilt the same every time), Testcontainers (databases and services that are born and die with the test) and per-PR previews (one deployment per PR, deleted when it closes).

A real ephemeral SUT: restful-booker-quality-suite/.github/workflows/tests.yml clones the SUT at commit 0046115, brings it up with docker compose up --build -d, polls /ping up to 30 times and, if something fails, dumps the container logs with if: failure(). When the job ends, the SUT dies with the runner.

What's lost when it dies: on-disk state, files you didn't upload, the cache, running processes and those processes' identity (PID, session). What survives: whatever you got out (artifacts, release assets, commits) and whatever you can recompute from pinned inputs.

Design 1, artifacts and receipts: upload everything you need to decide with actions/upload-artifact and if: ${{ !cancelled() }}, along with its SHA256SUMS. A receipt is the command, the input and output hashes and the exit code.

Design 2, pinned inputs: lockfiles (npm ci, uv run --locked in predictor-debugger), the tool version (astral-sh/setup-uv with version: "0.11.18"), the SUT commit (0046115), an image by digest (imagen@sha256:…) rather than by tag, and data verified against SHA256SUMS and a manifest (tools/fetch_data.py).

Design 3, idempotent checkpoints with a lock: each task writes its result atomically (a temp file, then mv) along with its hash; on resume, a task whose hash verifies is skipped; and a flock keeps two processes from doing the same task at once. Careful: checkpoints on the runner's disk die with the runner; to resume on another machine they have to get out first.

Design 4, verify in a clean environment: predictor-debugger/.github/workflows/reproduce.yml runs on a fresh ubuntu-24.04, downloads data-v1, verifies the hashes, recomputes and uses grep -q to require identical verdicts and the fingerprint. It lives in the repo, not on any machine, so it survives any executor. In the reviewed clone it covers rounds 1 and 2.

The real case, per the notes of predictor-debugger's repro-ia-20261026 release: a recomputation of rounds 1 to 4 from data-v1 on commit b918c62, without retraining or rerunning inference; “It was run by an AI assistant under my direction. It is not an independent review.” (original: «Lo ejecutó un asistente de IA bajo mi dirección. No es una revisión independiente.») The four fingerprints (EEC9-09E0-F77D, D506-F58F-3838, 6319-537B-7167, 681D-143B-64A3) match the original. Limitations it declares: “The data from a first run was lost. The 81 R1 files were regenerated: none is bit-for-bit identical to the published one; they differ by at most 8.9e-16” («Los datos de una primera corrida se perdieron. Los 81 archivos de la R1 se regeneraron: ninguno es idéntico bit a bit al publicado; difieren como máximo en 8,9e-16») and “R4 was interrupted and resumed from checkpoints” («La R4 se interrumpió y se retomó desde puntos de control»). The package contains 441 files and its SHA-256.

What the package says inside: results_scope.txt: “Original previous-run 81 arrays disappeared with ephemeral executor. Prior durable hashes/statistics recovered…” and “New generation explicitly identified as NEW RUN, not previous array recovery”. receipts/lock-hardening.json: “Global flock serializes scientific task/summary and per-task SHA/rows checked under lock for idempotent resume.” receipts/interruption.json: when the session was lost there were 6 verified tasks and 600 rows; the lock appeared free, “not sufficient alone to prove old driver absent”, and the policy was to relaunch nothing while the old process's identity was uncertain.

Four lessons: (1) whatever lived only on the executor was lost, and the hashes and statistics stored outside made comparison possible; (2) regenerating isn't recovering, and it's declared as a new run; (3) a free lock doesn't prove the old process died; (4) a matching fingerprint is the evidence that outlives everything else. The release doesn't mention CI: recomputing on a clean runner is a different path, the reproduce.yml one.

res.label: reproduce.yml — recomputation on a clean runner
docker image pull — images by digest

hands: Read the release: gh release view repro-ia-20261026 -R criguex/predictor-debugger.

Download the package into an empty folder and verify it before opening it: mkdir repro && cd repro && gh release download repro-ia-20261026 -R criguex/predictor-debugger && shasum -a 256 -c predictor_comparacion_canonica_R1-R4_final_20261026.zip.sha256 && unzip -q predictor_comparacion_canonica_R1-R4_final_20261026.zip -d x.

Read x/results_scope.txt, x/receipts/interruption.json and x/receipts/lock-hardening.json, and fill in a three-column table: what was lost, what was regenerated as a new run and what survived, with the file that says so.

Check the cheap fingerprint on your machine: git clone https://github.com/criguex/predictor-debugger.git && cd predictor-debugger && uv run --locked verify.py --saved mac, which should print fingerprint: EEC9-09E0-F77D.

Write your checkpointed run (Linux, or the CI runner; macOS doesn't ship flock): exec 9>.run.lock && flock -n 9 || exit 1; for each task, sha256sum -c out/$t.sha256 2>/dev/null && continue; otherwise compute into out/$t.tmp, do mv out/$t.tmp out/$t.json and sha256sum out/$t.json > out/$t.sha256. At the end, sha256sum out/*.json > SHA256SUMS and the fingerprint with sha256sum SHA256SUMS | cut -c1-12.

Write the workflow: runs-on: ubuntu-24.04, install with the lockfile, the run, echo "fingerprint: …" in the log and in $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY, and actions/upload-artifact with out/ and SHA256SUMS and if: ${{ !cancelled() }}.
Run the week's mutation: kill the run and relaunch it, and delete the cache and relaunch it.
crit: The workflow runs on ubuntu-24.04, installs with the lockfile and uploads an artifact with SHA256SUMS; the fingerprint is in the log and in the job summary.
You kill the run (gh run cancel <id>) and relaunch it (gh run rerun <id>): the fingerprint is the same, with both links.
With the cache deleted (gh cache delete --all) the fingerprint stays the same.

Locally, inside a container with out/ mounted as a volume, you docker kill it midway through the run, resume it, and the log shows it skipping the already-verified tasks; a second process with flock -n exits with an error while the first one is running.
Your release table cites, for each row, the file in the package or the line in the notes that backs it up.
m27.deliver: Clean-runner workflow with artifact, SHA256SUMS and fingerprint + checkpointed script under flock + evidence of the run killed and relaunched with the same fingerprint + table of what was lost and what survived in repro-ia-20261026.
m27.mut: Kill the container midway through the run (docker kill, or gh run cancel in CI) or delete the cache (gh cache delete --all), and relaunch. Write down beforehand what's going to be lost. If the fingerprint changes, if the resumed run repeats an already-verified task, or if two processes run at once, that's a finding: record it with its log.

levels: The evidence lives only on the runner or the container.
Uploads artifacts, but without hashes or only when everything passes.
Artifacts with SHA256SUMS and the fingerprint in the log and summary, even on failure.
Also, a third party downloads the artifact and verifies the fingerprint without your help.
Installs without a lockfile or with images by tag.
Lockfile, but tools or data not pinned.
Lockfile, tool version, commit or digest, and data with SHA256SUMS.
Also, the log prints the input versions and hashes as a receipt.
When cut off, it starts from scratch without knowing it.
Resumes, but repeats tasks or doesn't verify the hash.
Atomic checkpoints under flock; skips what's verified and shows it in the log.
Also proves that a second process can't get in and that a corrupt checkpoint gets recomputed.
There's no fingerprint.
The fingerprint changes between runs and isn't explained.
The same after killing and relaunching, and after deleting the cache.
Also the same on a second clean runner.

m10.title: Performance & Cloud (K6 · JMeter · AWS)
m10.mentor: First “it does the right thing,” then “it does it well under pressure” and “in the cloud.” Learn to read percentiles (p95/p99), not just passed/failed, and to validate serverless services with their quirks (cold starts).
m10.kid: It's one thing for the elevator to work with one person and another for it to work with twenty. The load test puts all twenty in.
obj: Write a k6 load test with thresholds and read p95/p99.
Add accessibility and visual regression without making the suite flaky.
Validate a serverless function end to end with traces.
theory: Types: load, stress, soak, spike; metrics: latency, throughput, p95/p99, error rate; SLI/SLO.
Observability with Grafana.
Serverless: cold starts, event-driven, traces with CloudWatch Logs Insights.

k6 2.x (2026) cleaned out the deprecated parts: k6 pause/resume/scale/status and the externally-controlled executor are gone; for the cloud it's k6 cloud run script.js. If an old tutorial uses those commands, translate them to ramping-vus/constant-arrival-rate.

Accessibility with axe-core (serious and critical violations) and visual regression with baselines generated on Linux with Docker: a baseline taken on macOS won't be picked up by CI (civica-playwright-challenge).
A performance budget with p95 over 20 samples (restful-booker-quality-suite, tests/performance/api.performance.spec.ts).
hands: A K6 load test against an endpoint with thresholds; interpret p95/p99.
Validate a Lambda end to end and trace a transaction in CloudWatch.
crit: The k6 thresholds make the run fail when they're exceeded.
The p95 budget is justified with data (for example, 20 samples).
The visual baselines are generated on the same system CI uses.
m10.deliver: K6 script with thresholds + performance report + serverless validation checklist.
m10.mut: Mutate the system's reality: inject latency or a 503 on purpose and check that your k6 thresholds fail.
m10.top: You inject latency or a 503 on purpose and show that your thresholds fail.

m20.title: Determinism — mocks, record/replay and hash-indexed fixtures
m20.mentor: A suite that depends on a third party or an AI changes when they change, not when your code changes. The way out is record and replay, with one rule: if the input changes, the old recording is useless and the test stays unverified, never green.
m20.kid: It's like recording the teacher's answer to study at home. But if you change the question, the old recording doesn't work anymore and you can't use it as if it were the new one.
obj: Record and replay responses from a third party or an AI, keyed by the request hash.
Show that a change in the input leaves the test unverified, never green.
Write an ADR with the failure policy.
theory: Test doubles (mock, stub, fake) to isolate third parties: civica-playwright-challenge uses a deterministic mock layer because IMDb blocks bots, and its real E2E skips with an honest reason (ADR 0002).
Record/replay: the first run records the service's or the judge's response; later runs replay it with no network or keys.

The key is a hash: in playwright-jev it's sha256(model, estado redactado, pregunta) (model, redacted state, question). Change one word and the fixture is missing, so the test stays unverified: it doesn't pass.
Same in agent-eval-jev and jev-test-impact: recordings are indexed by the hash of the exact request, so a changed question never reuses an old answer.
Three-valued verdicts: yes / no / ambiguous. Anything ambiguous or unverified never passes (playwright-jev, ADR 0001: fail-closed).
Write the decision down in an ADR: context, decision and consequences. playwright-jev documents five in docs/adr/.

res.label: civica's ADR 0002 — mocks as a fallback

hands: Clone playwright-jev and run JEV_MODE=replay npm run test:examples. Change one word in a judged text and show that the test ends up unverified, not green.
In your framework, record an external service's responses keyed by the request hash and replay them in CI with no network.
Write a one-page ADR with the record/replay decision and its failure policy.
crit: Changing one word of the input leaves the test unverified (never green), and you show it with the command's output.
CI runs with no keys or network, only recordings.
Every recording has its hash key and isn't reused if the request changes.
The ADR says what happens when a recording is missing.
m20.deliver: Suite with hash-keyed record/replay + a “change one word → unverified” demo + ADR.
m20.mut: Change one word in the judged text and check that the test ends up unverified, not green.
m20.top: The “change one word → unverified” test is part of CI itself.

m11.title: AI-Augmented QA — my differentiator
m11.mentor: This is what makes me different, and now it's yours. AI is the architect and generator of tests; you're the director who reviews every diff. It only works once you ALREADY know how to design and architect — that's why it comes at the end. The pattern: a “director” AI (e.g. Claude Code) that plans and keeps context, and an “executor” AI in the IDE (Copilot, Cursor…).
m11.kid: AI is a very fast helper that is sometimes wrong while sounding very sure. You're the one who checks before handing it in.
obj: Generate tests with a director AI and an executor AI, reviewing every diff.
Write a prompt with the 5 blocks (context, input, instruction, constraints, output).
Build a prompt pack with a review checklist.
theory: The core model: “the director AI plans, the IDE AI executes” — separating planning from execution works better and works with any pair of tools.
The 2 roles + the human: director AI = context and plan · IDE AI = executor sitting right on the code · you = judgment.
An instructions file for the IDE AI (e.g. copilot-instructions.md, or Cursor's rules) = “the IDE's CLAUDE.md”: the artifact that connects both AIs.
Anatomy of a good prompt (5 blocks): Context + Input + Instruction + Constraints + Expected output.
“Context before prompt”: a brilliant prompt on poor context gets you little.
Prompt packs: reusable recipes with <...> slots — “from 10 minutes to 1.”
The 3 context layers: CLAUDE.md (rules) · Persistent memory (facts about you) · Obsidian (knowledge).
Human-in-the-loop: “AI is confidently wrong” → ALWAYS review the diff.
A mental test for delegating: is the responsibility mine? Does it require business/risk judgment? Is it irreversible to the outside world? Is it mechanical work on a clear convention?
MCP: connecting tools to the model (e.g. Playwright MCP so the assistant drives a real browser). The Playwright + MCP + coding assistant combo shows up more and more in QA job postings.

res.label: Playwright MCP — the assistant drives the browser

hands: Generate a suite from an API contract or a user story with Claude + Copilot, reviewing the diff.
Build a prompt pack + a checklist for reviewing LLM output.
crit: Every generated test was run and has your review in the diff.
The prompt pack has marked slots and a usage example.
The review checklist catches at least one real LLM mistake.
m11.deliver: AI-generated suite (reviewed diff) + prompt pack + review checklist.
m11.mut: AI writes the checks too. When the code and its tests come from the same place, a green proves less than it seems: mutate it to find out whether it has teeth.
m11.top: You mutate the product and show that the generated tests turn red.

m14.title: AI-assisted QA I — the assistant tests, the person signs
m14.mentor: Today an assistant like Claude Code or Codex designs cases, runs the suite and even audits its own results. That doesn't take work away from me: it changes it. I decide which rules aren't negotiable, I put them where the assistant can't “forget” them (hooks and CI), and I only sign off on what has evidence that can be rerun.
m14.kid: Asking the robot “please don't touch that” is a request. Putting up a fence is a rule. Here you learn to put up fences and check that they have no holes.
obj: Put a non-negotiable rule in a hook or in CI, not in a prompt.
Attack your own hook with at least 10 attempts to get around it.
Leave rerunnable evidence: command, hash and exit code.
theory: Splitting the roles: the assistant designs, executes and audits; the person decides and signs. A green nobody can rerun doesn't get signed.

Rules live in hooks and CI, not in prompts: a prompt is a request the model can overlook; a hook that exits with code 2 is a wall. Real example: the Claude Code PreToolUse hook from war-paradigm's experiment 03 blocks any git push to main with exit 2.

Test the barrier the way you test the product (the WAR thread): its suite tries to sneak through with chained commands, refspecs and a bare git push while on main. And attacking it paid off: one mutation found two real holes (git -c and git --no-pager), fixed in commit 1b01c66; you'll work on it in AI-assisted QA II.
The assistant's context, versioned in the repo: CLAUDE.md for Claude Code, AGENTS.md for Codex. Commands, conventions and what's off-limits go there; never secrets.

Evidence = command + hash + exit code. In agent-eval-jev the judge's responses are stored with the exact hash of the request, and CI rebuilds the report and fails if it differs from the committed one.
Fail-safe by design: if the assistant or the AI service fails, the system does the conservative thing (run everything, mark unknown), never the comfortable one (skip tests, show green).
Declare authorship: in predictor-debugger a full reproduction was run by an assistant under human direction, and the README says so: it isn't an independent review.
hands: Ask your assistant (Claude Code or Codex) to design and run 5 new cases for your framework. Review the diff line by line and note what you accepted, what you corrected and why.
Write a hook that blocks a dangerous action (push to main, deleting test-results/, editing a snapshot) and test it with at least 10 attempts to get around it, including chained commands.
Leave an EVIDENCIA.md: for each run, the exact command, commit, input hash (shasum -a 256) and exit code.
crit: The hook exits with a non-zero code on every attempt to get around it and lets legitimate commands through.
Every claim in EVIDENCIA.md can be rerun with the written command and gives the same exit code.
The assistant's diff has your explicit review; no test was accepted without running it.
No critical rule lives only in a prompt.
m14.deliver: Tested hook + assistant-generated cases (reviewed diff) + EVIDENCIA.md with commands, hashes and exit codes.
m14.mut: Come up with 5 new ways to sneak a push to main through (an alias, a variable, git -C, an odd refspec) and add them to the hook's tests.
m14.top: You add 5 new ways to sneak a push to main to the tests of the war-paradigm 03 hook, and each one ends up blocked or reported as a hole.

m15.title: Mutation testing — kill rate, survivors and Stryker/PIT
m15.mentor: “Test the tester, mutate reality.” A green suite can be excellent or it can be asleep, and from the outside they look the same. The only way to know is to break something on purpose and see whether the suite shouts. This module is the thread through the whole course: this is where every technique you learned gets measured.
m15.kid: To find out if the guard is awake, you make a noise on purpose. If it shouts, it's awake (KILLED). If not, it's asleep (SURVIVED), and you have to say so.
obj: Classify mutants as baseline PASS, KILLED and SURVIVED without counting infrastructure failures.
Compute the kill rate and keep a ledger of survivors.
Run Stryker or PIT and resolve every survivor.
theory: You saw the WAR Paradigm's four steps (Generate → Mutate → Audit → Validate) and three verdicts (PASS, KILLED, SURVIVED) in module 2. Here you take them to a real suite and to the classic code mutation tools.
The baseline goes first and stays out of the score: if the baseline or the reset fails, you don't have dead mutants, you have an invalid experiment.
Kill rate = KILLED / (KILLED + SURVIVED). In war-paradigm 02: 5 out of 7, 71%. In the physics track: 54 KILLED and 3 SURVIVED out of 57 mutants, plus 27 baseline PASS (84 variants).

A SURVIVED doesn't get deleted or skipped: it's marked as an expected failure, printed in red and tracked in a ledger until someone fixes it. In experiment 02 both survivors are real bugs: an editor promotes themselves to admin (200), and a viewer creates a draft (201), a hole found while preparing this course.
Mutants as data: each one changes a single thing and leaves its JSON record (code revision and input hashes) as evidence.
Two mutants with the same output are equivalent: count them separately. In the physics track, the 54 KILLED correspond to 51 distinct behaviors.
Tools for mutating code: Stryker (JS/TS) and PIT (Java). WAR goes beyond code: it mutates business flows, physical laws or commands.
hands: Clone war-paradigm, run npm ci, npx playwright install --with-deps chromium and npm run demo:02, and explain in writing why the self-promotion-to-admin mutant survives.
On your framework from module 5: write 6 mutants as data (one change each: role, state, contract field, flow order), run them and classify them as PASS/KILLED/SURVIVED.
Run Stryker (or PIT if you're on Java) on a module with unit tests and compare its kill rate with what you expected.
crit: Your suite kills at least 5 of 6 mutants, and the one that survives is in the ledger with its cause.
Each scenario's JSON report includes the expected and observed state, the git revision and the input hashes.
The baseline runs first; a 5xx or a login failure comes out as INCONCLUSIVE or an invalid baseline, never as KILLED.
No survivor gets deleted, skipped or hidden.
m15.deliver: Catalog of mutants as data + PASS/KILLED/SURVIVED scoreboard + kill rate + survivor ledger.
m15.mut: Add two new mutants to the flow (publish without approval, approve your own document) and predict their verdict before running.
m15.top: You do war-paradigm 02's “Kill it yourself” exercise: you fix the rule in app/server.js and the self-grant survivor turns into KILLED.

m29.title: Running mutants — generate, run, classify and learn from every run
m29.mentor: Writing a mutant is easy. The hard part is running it without lying to yourself: if the baseline failed, if the server responded 500, or if the test never even got to attach evidence, that's not a killed mutant. Here you learn to classify with a conservative standard, to compute a kill rate you can defend in front of someone else, and to store what happened so the next run starts where it hurts.
m29.kid: You hide 6 broken toys in the box and ask the guard to find them. If it finds 5, its score is 5 out of 6. But if the lights went out in the room, that try doesn't count for or against: you write it down separately and do it again.
obj: Classify a mutant's result into one of five states and justify it with the observed code and the phase.
Compute a kill rate that excludes baseline and infrastructure, and reproduce it by hand from the evidence JSON.
Add mutants as data, with a single change and the prediction written down before running.
Use a ledger to reorder the next run without changing any verdict.
m29.pre: Mutation testing (test the tester), Playwright with TypeScript and API testing. Node 20 or later.
theory: The full cycle: generate (mutants as data) → run (baseline first, then a single change) → classify → score (kill rate) → record in a ledger → prioritize the next run.

Generating without scripts: in war-paradigm/experiments/02-mutants/tests/scenarios.ts each mutant is an object with a single change over the golden flow (role, body, step order or expired token) and the rejection the app must give: role-swap 403, drop-input 422, reorder 409, stale-token 401, boundary 422, self-grant 403 and viewer-create 403. In civica, generateSearchMutants(title) (src/support/mutations.ts) expands each seed title into three classes: equivalent (the result must not change), boundary (an edge that must keep working) and negative (the result must change).

Watch the name: in classic mutation testing (Stryker, PIT) an equivalent mutant is one no test can kill because it doesn't change behavior. In civica, equivalent is an input variation (INCEPTION, inception) that must give the same result; it's closer to a metamorphic relation.
Running in order: tests/scenario-runner.ts does the reset, the login and the unmutated baseline before mutating exactly one step. If any of that fails, that mutant tells you nothing about the suite.

Classifying (the Outcome type in tests/scenario-evidence.ts): KILLED if the mutation gets the expected 4xx; SURVIVED if it gets a 2xx; INCONCLUSIVE if it gets a 5xx or a rejection other than the expected one; INVALID_BASELINE if a precondition fails; INFRA_ERROR if the request or the runner fails, or if the test ended without attaching evidence (noEvidence()).

Kill rate = KILLED / (KILLED + SURVIVED). The other three states show up in the report and stay out of the score: “5/7 scored mutants killed · 2 survived · 0 excluded from score”. If you put them in the denominator, a server that's down lowers your kill rate; if you count them as KILLED, it raises it. Both are false.

Known survivors: self-grant and viewer-create carry a known field. They come out as KNOWN SURVIVOR, printed in red, and the default run stays green; with MUTANT_LAB_STRICT=1 (npm run test:strict) each of them makes the run fail. Once a bug is fixed, the scoreboard shows it as FIXED.

Per-scenario evidence in test-results/mutant-evidence.json: expected and observed state, phase, reason, git revision and SHA-256 of the app, the flow, the scenarios, the runner, the classifier, the spec and the lockfile, with randomSeed: null because the run uses no randomness.

The oracle's limit: it works at the HTTP level, plus a read of the role for self-grant. A correct status doesn't prove semantic equivalence, which is why the runner doesn't emit EQUIVALENT (README §Evidence, classification and score gate).

The ledger that learns (civica): reporters/mutationInsightsReporter.ts accumulates runs and failures per mutant in test-results/mutation-insights.json. prioritize() (src/support/mutationInsights.ts) gives weight 0 to those that ever failed, 1 to those never seen and 2 to those that always pass, with a stable order within each seed: it changes the order, never the verdict.

What that ledger doesn't do (it's in the code): failures is cumulative, so a mutant that failed once stays first forever; the reporter counts timedOut and interrupted as failures, without separating infrastructure the way war-paradigm does; and loadInsights() returns an empty ledger if the JSON is corrupt. In CI the ledger is uploaded as the mutation-insights artifact, but ci.yml doesn't download the one from the previous run, so every CI run starts with no memory.

Mutants that measure the auditor (civica, docs/AUDIT-POC.md §POC 3): on top of a hardened baseline, one defect is seeded per mutant (PII, three headers, an insecure cookie and the READ_SMS permission). Kill rate 6/6. Its ledger is kept separately, in test-results/audit-mutation-insights.json, so the two loops don't step on each other.

res.label: Petrović and Ivanković — State of Mutation Testing at Google

hands: Set up war-paradigm: git clone https://github.com/criguex/war-paradigm.git && cd war-paradigm && npm ci && npx playwright install --with-deps chromium.

Run npm run demo:02 and read the scoreboard. Open experiments/02-mutants/test-results/mutant-evidence.json and note, per scenario, expectedStatus, observedStatus, outcome and phase. Compute the kill rate by hand.
Run npm run test:strict -w experiments/02-mutants: the two known survivors make the run fail. Write down when you'd use strict mode and when the default.
Run npm run test:unit -w experiments/02-mutants and read the five cases in tests/unit/scenario-evidence.test.ts. Add one: if 403 was expected and 404 arrives, the result has to be INCONCLUSIVE.

Add two mutants in tests/scenarios.ts and commit your prediction before running. For example { id: "viewer-publish", name: "viewer-publish", expect: 403, step: "publish", as: "viewer" } and a 2-character title in create with expect: 422.
“Kill it yourself”: change editMember in app/server.js to (actor) => actor.role === "admin", run npm run demo:02 and check that self-grant comes out FIXED. Then remove the known field.

Set up civica: git clone https://github.com/criguex/civica-playwright-challenge.git && cd civica-playwright-challenge && npm ci && npx playwright install --with-deps chromium. Run npm run test:mutation twice and compare test-results/mutation-insights.json between runs.

Look at the order without running anything: npx playwright test --project=mutation --list. Edit the ledger, set "failures": 1 on a mutant that's last in its seed, and list again: it should move up to first place in that seed.

Auditor: npm run test:audit -- securityMutants and cat test-results/audit/security-mutants.json. Add a mutant in src/audit/securityMutations.ts (for example, removing X-Frame-Options) and note whether it dies. m21.title: Mutants that learn — ledger, prioritization and mutants that measure the auditor
m21.mentor: Running mutants once is a snapshot. Storing what happened and using it in the next run is a movie: first the ones that failed before, then the new ones, and last the ones that always pass. The same idea works for measuring a security auditor: you seed the defect and see whether it finds it.
m21.kid: If in the last game the goalkeeper missed the shots to the left, in practice you shoot to the left first.

theory: In civica-playwright-challenge there are three mutant classes (equivalent, boundary, negative) and a prioritize() that sorts them: first the ones that failed before, then the never-seen ones, and last the ones that always pass.

A reporter writes test-results/mutation-insights.json: that's the ledger. In civica that file is in .gitignore and only exists as a CI artifact; for the loop to learn across CI runs you have to restore that artifact.
Reordering must not break determinism: it changes the order, not each mutant's verdict.
Mutants that measure the auditor: on top of a hardened baseline, one security defect is seeded per mutant (PII, headers, cookies, Android permissions). In civica's POC 3 the kill rate is 6/6.
If a new mutant survives, that's a finding about the auditor: it gets reported, and the mutant isn't tweaked until it dies.
Next step on civica's roadmap: metamorphic relations, for example “the results for X contain the results for a prefix of X.”

m18.title: CI failure triage and impact-based test selection
m18.mentor: A red pipeline is a list of questions, and only some of them are bugs. My rule with these two tools: deterministic rules decide whatever they can, the model only weighs in on what's ambiguous and, when in doubt, you do the safe thing. Triage never turns a red green, and the selector never skips a test out of uncertainty.
m18.kid: When several tests fail at once, a good mail carrier puts each letter in its mailbox: a real mistake, bad luck, the network or the wrong data. And if you changed the car's mirror you don't check the engine; but if you're not sure what the change touched, you check everything.
obj: Classify 10 failures into the 5 classes (regression, flaky, environment, test-data, unknown), each one with the evidence that backs it up.
Predict which rule in src/classifier.ts decides each demo failure before running the tool, and get it right or explain every difference.

m18.pre: The CI/CD and pipelines module, Playwright JSON or JUnit reporters and Node 22 or newer. No keys: both labs replay recorded Jev responses.
theory: Five classes: regression (the product changed), flaky (same code, different result), environment (network, dependency, runner), test-data (fixtures or seed data) and unknown (no evidence: a person looks at it first).

Rules in order (src/classifier.ts): (1) failed and passed on a retry in the same run → flaky; (2) an infrastructure marker (ECONNREFUSED, DNS, net::ERR_*, 502/503/504…) with no changes to the test's own code → environment, and a bare 500 doesn't count; (3) with at least minHistory runs, the result flipped two or more times → flaky; (4) it always passed, now fails on every attempt and the diff touches app code, not the test or its data → regression; (5) everything else goes to Jev.

Test-data is never decided by a rule: telling “the fixture changed” from “the product changed” is a question of meaning. Jev answers with probabilities; below 0.75 the failure stays unknown and goes to a person. Before sending anything, tokens, JWTs, emails, card-shaped numbers and home-directory paths are redacted (src/redact.ts).

Confidence moves around and the service goes down. The same input came back with 0.69, 0.71, 0.78 and 0.84 against the 0.75 threshold, and one afternoon only 17 of 126 calls succeeded because of HTTP 429. That's why it fails open: unknown · unverified, no guessing. In the Action, fail-on can make the step fail, never make it pass.

Impact-based selection (jev-test-impact): the import graph decides the unit tests. Black-box tests don't import the code they exercise, so they don't trust a “no” from the graph and go to Jev with a 0.2 threshold, deliberately low. @smoke always runs, and a change in fullSuiteOn (lockfiles, configs) runs everything.

Fail-safe: any Jev failure runs the full suite, and the full suite keeps running on main and every night. Across 20 commits with 6 regressions and 15 broken tests: 69.9% fewer tests and 0 of 15 escaped; the unsafe policy skipped 77% and let 4 of 15 escape. It's a small app: evidence, not a guarantee.
